newsitem.title: USA: US jobless claims may signal labor market weakness.
newsitem.headline: US jobless claims may signal labor market weakness.

text.p: A sharp jump in U.S. jobless claims last week may indicate developing weakness in the labor market, although it is too soon to tell for sure, analysts said.
On Wednesday morning, the Labor Department said 366,000 people initiated claims for state unemployment benefits in the week ended December 28, up from a revised 344,000 the week before.
U.S. economists in a Reuters poll had forecast 334,000 new claims would be filed.
Last week's initial, or unrevised reading on claims came in at 335,000, which was below most economists' forecasts and instilled some fear the labor market might be tightening.
But the subsequent upward revision to last week's number and the jump in this week's eased any developing fears, said Marilyn Schaja, money market economist at DLJ Securities Corp.
"We are starting to see a weakening trend developing," Schaja said. "That's what you have to get out of this number."
The unexpected rise in claims cheered the Treasury market, spurring a quarter-point rise in the bellwether long bond in the immediate aftermath of the report.
Schaja said that reaction was justified, particularly because "the market had a really bad day on Tuesday." She cautioned, however, that "you can't read too much into one week's claims statistic."
Other analysts said the market's reaction may have been a bit too reflexive, since jobless claims tends to be a volatile statistic.
"It would be a slightly exaggerated reaction at this point," said Asha Bangalore, an economist at Northern Trust.
The government has trouble seasonally adjusting jobless claims around the holiday, analysts pointed out.
"What happens in this time of year is you have these holiday shock weeks, people hiring and laying off," said Bangalore.
Bangalore said the holiday hiring and firing picture would remain unclear for the next few weeks.
"It's premature to pronounce you have some softness developing in the labor market," she said.
With the December payrolls data coming up next week, Thursday's jobless claims report probably has few implications for monetary policy, analysts said.

"This rise in jobless claims should begin to give (dovish central bankers) some comfort, but the hawks are probably feeling as uneasy as ever," said Dan Seto, senior economist at The Nikko Securities Co International Inc.
Seto said the higher four-week claims average suggests that labor market tightness has eased somewhat, but the report is "certainly not conclusive evidence."
